stem: A political party is a group of people who come together to:
options: Contest elections and hold power in the government
solution: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government.

stem: A political party is a group of people who agree on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to:
solution: Parties agree on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to promoting the collective good; since there can be different views on what is good, parties try to persuade people why their policies are better.

stem: The three components of a political party are:
options: The leaders, the active members and the followers
The rich, the poor and the middle class
The centre, states and local bodies
solution: A political party has three components: the leaders, the active members and the followers.

stem: A party is known by which of the following?
options: Which part of society it stands for, the policies it supports and the interests it upholds
solution: A party is known by which part of society it stands for, the policies it supports, and the interests it upholds.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the functions parties perform in a democracy?
options: Parties put forward different policies and programmes
Parties directly run the courts and deliver judgments
solution: Parties contest elections, put forward policies, make laws, form and run governments, play the role of opposition, shape public opinion and provide access to government machinery — but they do not run the courts.

stem: Those parties that lose elections play the role of:
options: Opposition — voicing different views and criticising the government for its failures
solution: Parties that lose elections play the role of opposition to the parties in power, by voicing different views and criticising the government for its failures or wrong policies.

stem: Parties shape public opinion by:
options: Raising and highlighting issues, and having pressure groups and movements linked to them
solution: Parties shape public opinion; they raise and highlight issues. Parties have lakhs of members and activists spread all over the country, and many of the pressure groups are the extensions of political parties.

stem: Parties provide people access to government machinery and welfare schemes by:
options: Being a link between ordinary citizens and government machinery, which people find easier to approach
solution: Parties provide people access to government machinery and welfare schemes implemented by governments; for an ordinary citizen it is easy to approach a local party leader than a government officer.

stem: Why do we need political parties? The absence of parties would mean:
options: Every candidate in elections would be independent, no promises of major policy change, no one responsible for how the country is run
solution: If there were no parties, every candidate would be independent; no one could make promises about major policy changes; the government would be formed but its utility would remain uncertain; and no one would be responsible for how the country is run.

stem: Political parties are a necessary condition for a democracy because they:
options: Emerge as societies become large and complex, needing agencies to gather diverse views and present them to the government
solution: As societies became large and complex, they needed some agency to gather different views on various issues and present them to the government; parties fill this need, making them a necessary condition of representative democracy.

stem: A system in which only one party is allowed to control and run the government is called a:
solution: In some countries only one party is allowed to control and run the government — this is a one-party system, as in China; it is not a good option because it does not allow healthy competition.

stem: The one-party system is not considered a good democratic option because:
options: It does not allow any meaningful competition or a democratic choice to citizens
solution: The one-party system is not a good option because this is not a democratic option — any democratic system must allow at least two parties to compete in elections and provide a fair chance for the competing parties to come to power.

stem: A system in which power usually changes between two main parties is called a:
solution: In a two-party system, power usually changes between two main parties; several other parties may exist and contest but only the two main parties have a serious chance of winning majority. The USA and the UK are examples.

stem: Examples of countries with a two-party system are:
options: The United States of America and the United Kingdom
solution: The United States of America and the United Kingdom are examples of two-party systems.

stem: A system in which several parties compete for power, and more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power, is called a:
solution: In a multi-party system, several parties compete for power and more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power either on their own strength or in alliance with others; India has a multi-party system.

stem: When several parties in a multi-party system come together to contest elections and win power, it is called a(n):
solution: When several parties in a multi-party system join hands for the purpose of contesting elections and winning power, it is called an alliance or a front — for example, India had the NDA, UPA and the Left Front.

stem: The multi-party system often appears very messy and leads to political instability, but it allows:
options: A variety of interests and opinions to enjoy political representation
solution: The multi-party system often leads to political instability; at the same time it allows a wide variety of interests and opinions to enjoy political representation.

stem: According to the chapter, why did India adopt a multi-party system?
options: The social and geographical diversity of India is not easily absorbed by two or even three parties
solution: India evolved a multi-party system because the social and geographical diversity in such a large country is not easily absorbed by two or even three parties; no system is ideal for all countries and situations.

stem: According to the Constitution and law, a party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a State and wins at least two seats is recognised as a:
solution: A party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a State and wins at least two seats is recognised as a State party.

stem: A party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four States and wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha is recognised as a:
solution: A party that secures at least six per cent of total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four States, and wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha, is recognised as a national party.

stem: The Election Commission treats recognised parties in a special manner by giving them a unique:
options: Symbol, and access to free election broadcasts on state television and radio
solution: The Election Commission registers political parties and gives them a unique symbol; only officially recognised parties are allotted these symbols and enjoy privileges like free time on state TV and radio during elections.

stem: The Indian National Congress (INC) is one of the oldest parties in the world, founded in:
solution: The Indian National Congress, popularly known as the Congress Party, is one of the oldest and most influential parties, founded in 1885; it played a dominant role in Indian politics after Independence.

stem: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was founded in 1980 by reviving the erstwhile:
solution: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was founded in 1980 by reviving the erstwhile Bharatiya Jana Sangh, established in 1951 by Syama Prasad Mukherjee.

stem: Which of the following is a national party that draws inspiration from the ideas of Mahatma Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar and stands for the interests of Dalits (Bahujan Samaj)?
solution: The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), formed in 1984 under the leadership of Kanshi Ram, seeks to represent and secure power for the bahujan samaj — the Dalits, Adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities — drawing inspiration from Sahu Maharaj, Mahatma Phule, Periyar Ramaswami Naicker and Ambedkar.

stem: The Communist Party of India (Marxist) — CPI(M) — believes in:
options: Marxism-Leninism, and supports socialism, secularism and democracy while opposing imperialism and communalism
solution: CPI(M) believes in Marxism-Leninism; it supports socialism, secularism and democracy, and opposes imperialism and communalism. It has been strong in West Bengal, Kerala and Tripura.

stem: Parties that are present in only some states are called:
solution: Other than national parties, most of the major parties of the country are classified as State parties (commonly referred to as regional parties), though some like the DMK or the Biju Janata Dal are conscious of their national role.

stem: Over the last three decades, the number and strength of regional parties in India has:
options: Expanded, making the Parliament of India politically more and more diverse
solution: Over the last three decades, the number and strength of regional parties has expanded, making the Parliament of India politically more and more diverse; no single national party has been able to secure a clear majority in the Lok Sabha on its own for a long period.

stem: The rise of regional parties has led to the era of:
solution: The growing strength of regional parties has led to a genuine federal distribution of power and to the formation of coalition governments at the Centre.

stem: The first challenge faced by political parties is the:
options: Lack of internal democracy within parties
solution: The first challenge is the lack of internal democracy within parties — power tends to be concentrated in the hands of one or a few leaders at the top; parties do not keep membership registers, hold organisational meetings or conduct internal elections regularly.

stem: The second challenge that political parties face is the:
options: Dynastic succession — top positions being controlled by members of one family, which is unfair to others and bad for democracy
solution: The second challenge is that of dynastic succession — since most parties do not practise open and transparent procedures, those close to the leaders or their families get preference, an unfair practice bad for democracy.

stem: The third challenge to parties, especially during elections, is the growing role of:
options: Money and muscle power, with parties nominating those who can raise money or win by any means
solution: The third challenge is the growing role of money and muscle power in parties, especially during elections; parties tend to nominate those candidates who have or can raise lots of money, and sometimes support criminals who can win elections.

stem: The fourth challenge is that parties often do not offer a meaningful choice to voters because:
options: In order to offer a meaningful choice, parties must be significantly different, but the differences among all major parties on fundamental issues have narrowed
solution: The fourth challenge is that very often parties do not seem to offer a meaningful choice to the voters — in order to offer a meaningful choice, parties must be significantly different, yet the ideological differences among major parties have come down in most parts of the world.

stem: One suggestion to reform political parties is a law to regulate the internal affairs of parties, which was made through:
options: The Representation of the People Act
solution: A law was passed (the anti-defection law) to prevent elected MLAs and MPs from changing parties, requiring a member who defects to lose their seat, in order to check the practice of defection driven by the lure of office or money.

stem: The anti-defection law provides that if any MLA or MP changes parties, he or she will:
options: Lose the seat in the legislature
solution: The Constitution was amended (anti-defection law) to prevent elected members from changing parties; now if any MLA or MP changes parties, he or she will lose the seat in the legislature — this has helped reduce defection but also made members submissive to party leadership.

stem: The Supreme Court passed an order to reduce the influence of money and criminals, making it mandatory for every candidate contesting elections to:
options: File an affidavit giving details of their property and criminal cases pending against them
solution: Following a Supreme Court order, it is now mandatory for every candidate who contests elections to file an affidavit giving details of his property and criminal cases pending against him, submitted to the Election Commission.

stem: The Election Commission passed an order making it necessary for political parties to:
options: Hold their organisational elections and file their income tax returns
solution: The Election Commission passed an order making it necessary for political parties to hold their organisational elections and file their income tax returns — though parties do this as a formality.

stem: Reservation of one-third seats for women in party organisational positions and legislatures is a suggestion aimed at reforming parties to make them:
options: More democratic and representative of women
solution: It has been suggested that a law should be made to have at least one-third tickets given to women candidates; a quota for women in the decision-making bodies of the party would make parties more internally democratic and representative.

stem: There should be a state funding of elections, according to one suggestion, meaning:
options: The state should give parties money to meet election expenses (in kind or cash)
Only the ruling party gets money
Elections should be privately funded only
solution: One suggestion is that the government should give parties money to support their election expenses; this state funding could be in kind (petrol, paper, telephone) or in cash on the basis of votes secured in the last election.

stem: Two ways in which people and civil society can reform political parties are:
options: Through public pressure (petitions, publicity, agitations) and by ordinary citizens joining parties to influence them
solution: People can reform parties by putting pressure through petitions, publicity and agitations, and those who wish to reform parties can join them; the quality of democracy depends on the degree of public participation.

stem: The chapter cautions that any legal reforms of parties are likely to be counterproductive if:
options: Laws are made without the involvement and consent of the parties themselves and public opinion is not mobilised
solution: Legal ways of reforming parties are not very successful; carefully devised changes in laws can help discourage wrong tendencies, but ultimately reforms depend on public awareness, media and party involvement.

stem: The main criticism against the anti-defection law is that it has:
options: Reduced the role of individual members and made them submissive to party leadership, since they cannot express independent views
solution: While the anti-defection law reduced defection, it has also made MPs and MLAs completely dependent on party leadership; they cannot vote or speak against the party line, reducing their independence.

stem: Which of the following statements about the Indian National Congress after Independence is correct?
options: It was a broad-based centrist party that played a dominant role in Indian politics, especially in the decades after Independence
solution: The Congress played a dominant role in Indian politics at the national and state level after Independence; it is a centrist party (neither the left nor the right) in its ideological orientation and supports secularism and welfare of weaker sections.

stem: Which of the following best explains 'partisan'?
options: A person who is strongly committed to a party, group or faction, marked by a tendency to take a side and unable to see any good point in the other's position
solution: A partisan is a person who is strongly committed to a party, group or faction; partisanship is marked by a tendency to take a side and an inability to see any good points in another's position.

stem: The term 'ruling party' refers to:
options: The political party that runs the government
solution: The ruling party is the political party that runs the government, as distinct from the opposition parties.

stem: The recognised parties in India — those given a symbol and other facilities by the Election Commission — are of which two kinds?
solution: Recognised parties are classified as either 'national' parties or 'State' parties, based on the proportion of votes and seats they secure, and are given a reserved symbol.

stem: The most serious challenge faced by parties, according to the chapter, requires reforms that make parties more:
solution: The challenges of lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, and lack of meaningful choice all point to the need for reforms that make parties more internally democratic, transparent and accountable to citizens.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE about coalition governments in India?
options: They have become common at the Centre since no single party has been able to win a clear majority in the Lok Sabha for long periods
solution: Coalition governments have become common at the Centre; the rise of regional parties and the inability of a single national party to secure a clear majority in the Lok Sabha for long periods gave rise to alliances such as the NDA, UPA and the Left Front.

stem: Parties are so central to democracy that it is common to hear people say that parties are:
options: The most visible institutions of a democracy, and that they are what is wrong with democracy — they generate disrespect but are indispensable
solution: Political parties are one of the most visible institutions of a democracy; for most ordinary citizens, democracy is equal to political parties. Yet parties have become identified with social and political divisions — they are indispensable but need reform.

stem: The rise of coalition politics and regional parties has, on balance, strengthened Indian federalism by:
options: Leading to a genuine sharing of power between the Centre and the states and giving regional aspirations political representation
solution: The greater role of regional parties in coalition governments has led to a more genuine federal sharing of power between the Centre and the States, and has given regional aspirations political representation.

stem: The Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) was formed in 1999 following a split in which party?
solution: The Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) was formed in 1999 following a split in the Congress Party; it espouses democracy, Gandhian secularism, equity, social justice and federalism, and has been a major party in Maharashtra.
